messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 78
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Database Administrator
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 73

John is a 78-year-old retired database administrator who has lived most of his life in the midwest. He married young and had two children, but after a tumultuous relationship with his ex-wife, they divorced amicably about twenty years ago. John lives alone now in a modest home filled with books on technology and a collection of vinyl records he's amassed over decades. John’s PTSD symptoms stem from a life-threatening illness he experienced five years ago when he was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia. The diagnosis came as a shock; he had always considered himself healthy, aside from the occasional cold or flu. The chemotherapy treatments left him weak and nauseous for months, and there were several times during his treatment when he thought he might not survive. Now, five years post-diagnosis, John often finds himself caught in the grips of intrusive thoughts about that time. He can vividly recall the sterile smell of the hospital and the sensation of being hooked up to IV lines. His hands shake sometimes as he thinks about how close he came to death. At night, his sleep is fragmented; he wakes frequently with a start, drenched in sweat, heart pounding from nightmares where he relives those terrifying moments. John’s job as a database administrator required meticulous attention to detail and long hours of sitting at his desk. He often worked late into the evenings, ensuring systems were running smoothly. Now, even though retired, John still feels compelled to check things repeatedly; for instance, he will often double-check if he locked doors or turned off lights multiple times before going out. This compulsion has extended to more mundane aspects of life as well; he meticulously organizes his medications and schedules appointments with his doctors months in advance. The hyperarousal symptoms are particularly challenging for John. He is easily startled and jumpy, especially when there’s any kind of sudden noise or movement around him. He avoids news programs that discuss health issues because they trigger a cascade of memories about his illness and treatment. Even though he enjoys gardening, he tends to avoid the community garden events where he used to socialize, preferring instead to work alone in his backyard. John is also grappling with intense guilt about how his illness affected his family. He remembers feeling helpless when his children had to take time off work to care for him during chemotherapy treatments. The thought of burdening them again terrifies him and exacerbates his anxiety. Sometimes he has flashbacks, particularly vivid ones where he sees the worried faces of his kids looking at him in the hospital. In the past year, John has started attending a support group for cancer survivors. Though it’s hard for him to open up about his feelings, being around others who understand what he went through has provided some comfort. Still, there are days when he feels isolated and disconnected from the world. Simple tasks that once gave him joy now feel overwhelming. John’s symptoms have affected his daily life significantly. While he values his independence and remains active in his hobbies, the constant vigilance and fear of another health crisis loom large over everything he does. He tries to keep a journal as a way to process his thoughts and emotions but often finds himself staring at blank pages, words stuck in his throat. Despite these challenges, John maintains a sense of resilience that has been a hallmark of his character throughout life. He still reads voraciously and keeps up with technological advancements, though he admits it’s harder now to focus for long periods without feeling distracted by intrusive thoughts or physical symptoms like heart palpitations. John is slowly learning coping mechanisms to navigate through the day-to-day challenges, finding small moments of peace in the familiar hum of his record player or the steady rhythm of typing on his computer keyboard.
